title: Early Genesis — Geography and Uncertainty
subtitle: Explore Eden, Ararat, Shinar, and Babel without pretending uncertain or theological geography is a modern GPS layer.

chapters.title: Eden — deliberately unpinned
chapters.description: The atlas treats Eden differently from an excavated city. Genesis names rivers, but the description cannot responsibly be converted into a single established coordinate. Search and evidence panels remain available even when no map pin is drawn.

chapters.title: The mountains of Ararat
chapters.description: Genesis says “mountains of Ararat,” not “Mount Ararat.” The map therefore uses a broad highland anchor and explicitly avoids claiming a landing site.

chapters.title: Shinar and Babel
chapters.description: Shinar is shown as a regional Mesopotamian anchor. Babylon is locatable as an ancient city, while the tower narrative is presented as a textual event rather than an archaeological pin for a specific structure.

title: Abraham — Journey of Promise
subtitle: From southern Mesopotamia through Haran into Canaan, with route certainty and disputed geography made visible.

chapters.title: Ur
chapters.description: The conventional identification places Ur of the Chaldeans at ancient Ur in southern Mesopotamia. The city is real and well excavated; linking the patriarchal family specifically to this site remains a historical-geographic judgment.

chapters.title: Ur → Haran → Canaan
chapters.description: The moving traveler follows the sequence named in Genesis. The connecting curves are schematic geographic reconstructions; the app never claims these are the exact roads walked by Abraham.

chapters.title: Shechem
chapters.description: Unlike Eden or Sodom, ancient Shechem can be mapped with high geographic confidence at Tell Balata. The archaeological city and the Genesis episode are kept conceptually distinct.

chapters.title: Hebron and Mamre
chapters.description: Hebron is a secure ancient location; Mamre’s specific traditional site is less certain. The interface presents both without flattening their confidence levels.

chapters.title: Sodom — no definitive pin
chapters.description: The atlas records competing Dead Sea proposals instead of choosing an archaeological site without sufficient consensus. This is a deliberate design feature, not missing data.

chapters.title: Moriah
chapters.description: A separate journey illustrates the later Temple Mount identification of Moriah. Because Genesis speaks of the “land of Moriah,” the route and endpoint are labeled as interpretive rather than archaeologically proven for Abraham.

title: Isaac — Wells, Gerar, and Beersheba
subtitle: A more geographically concentrated patriarchal story centered in the southern Canaan/Negev zone.

chapters.title: Gerar
chapters.description: Gerar cannot be mapped with the same confidence as Hebron or Shechem. The atlas uses a candidate location near Tell Haror and marks the identification as possible.

chapters.title: Toward Beersheba
chapters.description: Genesis names Isaac’s movement to Beersheba. Intermediate well locations are intentionally not assigned confident modern coordinates.

chapters.title: Beersheba
chapters.description: Tell es-Seba is the principal archaeological anchor for biblical Beersheba, although its best-known remains are later than the patriarchal narratives.

title: Jacob — Exile, Return, and Israel
subtitle: Follow Jacob from Beersheba to Bethel and Haran, then back through Gilead and the Jabbok into Canaan.

chapters.title: Bethel
chapters.description: Jacob’s dream is tied to Bethel/Luz. The Beitin-area identification is strong enough to map, while still labeled probable rather than absolute.

chapters.title: To Haran and back
chapters.description: The story animation connects the named geographic sequence but does not imply knowledge of Jacob’s exact roads across Syria and upper Mesopotamia.

chapters.title: The Jabbok and Peniel
chapters.description: The Jabbok is securely identified with the Zarqa River. Peniel, however, remains a proposed local site. The map deliberately gives the river and settlement different confidence levels.

chapters.title: Shechem and Bethel
chapters.description: Jacob’s return sequence links Succoth, Shechem, Bethel, and eventually Hebron. Established ancient cities stand alongside uncertain Transjordanian stops.

title: Joseph — From Dothan to Egypt
subtitle: The Genesis story expands from the Canaanite hill country into Egypt and the eastern Delta.

chapters.title: Dothan
chapters.description: Tell Dothan gives the Joseph narrative one of its more confidently mapped locations. The story then moves into a long unrecorded travel corridor toward Egypt.

chapters.title: Caravan toward Egypt
chapters.description: Genesis does not identify the merchants’ precise path. The animation therefore shows a broad geographic corridor and labels the route certainty as unknown.

chapters.title: On / Heliopolis
chapters.description: On is securely identified with Heliopolis. It enters the Genesis story through Joseph’s marriage to Asenath, daughter of Potiphera priest of On.

chapters.title: Goshen
chapters.description: Goshen is shown in the eastern Nile Delta as a broad regional anchor. Exact boundaries are not presented as settled.

chapters.title: Jacob comes to Egypt
chapters.description: The final Genesis movement brings Jacob’s household from Beersheba into Egypt. The route is schematic, while the narrative sequence is explicit.
